sections.html:
Hills roll up toward the Blue Ridge in this central Piedmont county of 343 square miles, home to 36,254 people in 2020. Its seat is the Town of Orange, and Gordonsville is the second town. Addresses also use names like Barboursville, Lake of the Woods, Locust Grove, Rapidan, Rhoadesville, Unionville, Somerset and Montpelier Station.

Many parcels are acreage, so land size and land use status can weigh as heavily as the house on a bill or a sale price. Mention the acreage and any land use enrollment in your first conversation with a buyer.

The county created a Real Estate Assessment Department in 2024 to set values. The Treasurer bills and collects. The department says its purpose is a fair spread of the tax burden, and state rules call for assessment at 100 percent of fair market value.

OfficeWhat it handlesHow to reach it
Real Estate Assessment DepartmentAnnual assessments and appeals intake(540) 672-6173, 112 West Main Street, Orange, VA 22960
TreasurerBills, payments, late payment rulesCounty main line (540) 672-3313, P.O. Box 111, Orange, VA 22960
Board of EqualizationReviews assessment complaintsThrough the assessment department, (540) 672-6173

For any question about value, call the assessment department number above.

sections.h2: Due dates and the fiscal year billing change
sections.html:
Two bills a year: half is due December 5 and half is due June 5.

Billing now follows the county's July 1 to June 30 fiscal year (Virginia Code 58.1-3010), after a short interim period that ran January 1 to June 30, 2025. The December and June bills are unchanged in name, yet December now opens the year.

  • September to October: the first bill of the fiscal year is mailed.
  • December 5: first half due, based on the January 1 assessment and the rate set the previous spring.
  • Spring: reassessment notices go out, with the county aiming for early May.
  • June 5: second half due, resting on the earlier January 1 assessment and the rate set a year before.

Treat a reassessment notice as information only, not something to pay. The new value reaches a bill the following December, so a June payment made at closing may rest on an older value than the notice in your mailbox.

Pay late and you owe a 10 percent penalty, plus yearly interest of 10 percent charged on the tax and the penalty together. For a December bill the interest clock starts December 6 and adds up on the first day of every month after that (Code of Virginia 58.1-3916).

A check in the mail counts as on time only with a Post Office postmark dated by the deadline. Your own postage meter stamp will not do.

  • No waiver for a missing bill, a wrong mailing address or a misread date.
  • An exception exists for a medically determinable impairment on the due date, if you pay within 30 days.
  • No penalty if the lateness came only from an error by the Treasurer or the Commissioner of the Revenue.

Selling with a past-due bill? The closing agent will ask for a payoff covering penalty and interest.

Begin by contacting the Real Estate Assessment Department and filing the county's appeal application. When that review leaves you unsatisfied, the Board of Equalization is next.

The circuit court appoints the board. It is made up mostly of local freeholders, and at least 30 percent of its members must be current or former real estate, construction, financial or legal professionals. Its powers come from Chapter 32, Article 14 of Title 58.1. Your mailed notice explains how to file.

State law, under Va. Code 58.1-3379, presumes the assessor's value is correct and puts the burden on the taxpayer. Staff are not choosing values to move taxes up or down. The market drives value, while the Board of Supervisors sets the rate each spring.

Gather proof before you call: comparable sales, photos of problems and repair estimates. Ask the department which forms and attachments the board expects, and file early enough that a hearing does not collide with your closing.

The county's claim for unpaid real estate tax outranks everything else recorded against the house. That is why the Treasurer's balance is settled out of your proceeds before the buyer gets clear title. Virginia Code 58.1-3340 sends the money to taxes first, whether the buyer or a foreclosure trustee is paying, and leaves the split of the current year to your contract.

On the deed itself, a state grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of consideration applies under Va. Code 58.1-802. Sellers normally cover it, though the parties may agree to something different.

If the parcel is enrolled in land use assessment, ask the county what happens to the special valuation when the land changes hands. The county also runs tax relief for the elderly, for disabled owners and for disabled former service members, and each program has its own application.

Two things catch sellers here: when the two bills land, and how yearly reassessment shifts the figure on the page.

  • Parcel size: acreage and land use status can change both the bill and the sale process.
  • Timing: the December and June due dates can fall in the middle of a contract period.
  • Lag: a new assessed value does not reach a bill until the following December.

Values are redone every year starting in 2025, so a house you bought a few years back may be carried at a quite different figure today. Ask the assessment department for the current figure before you price the house.

A workable order before listing: ask the Treasurer which bill is paid, confirm acreage and land use with the assessment department, give the title company your latest bill and notice, and pick a closing date relative to the next due date so the proration can go into the contract.

A direct cash sale can help when an estate wants to avoid repairs, showings and months on the market. The tax payoff works the same way in any sale, so ask the county for a balance first.

Have the street address or tax map number, the newest bill and the latest assessment notice in front of you for each call. With those, the Treasurer can read out what is paid and what is open, and the assessment department can confirm acreage, land use and improvements on file. If the house has had an addition or a teardown, say so, since the department tracks those changes and they can shift the value.

Send the payoff to your title company in writing so nothing relies on a phone memory. A written figure also gives you something to compare against the settlement statement on closing day, when a missing line is much easier to catch.

faqs.q: When are Orange County, VA real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due December 5 and the second half June 5. December opens the county's fiscal year.

faqs.q: Does Orange County reassess every year?
faqs.a: Yes, annually since 2025, with notices going out in spring. Those notices are not tax bills.

faqs.q: Can Orange County waive a late tax penalty?
faqs.a: Seldom. A missed bill or a misread date is not grounds. The narrow exceptions are a medical impairment and a mistake made by a county office.

faqs.q: Who do I call about an Orange County assessment?
faqs.a: Phone the Real Estate Assessment Department, (540) 672-6173, or visit 112 West Main Street in Orange.

faqs.q: Do I pay Orange County property tax when I sell?
faqs.a: The closing agent pays what you owe out of your proceeds, since the county's lien comes first. Your contract normally divides the current year between you and the buyer.
